https://www.irishdentist.ie/energy-drink.text: Politics July 20, 2026 Energy drinks banned for under 16s: why England says stop and what can change in Italy They promise immediate energy, concentration, resistance to tiredness. They have brightly colored cans, aggressive names and a now constant presence in sports, video games, social networks and influencer content. For many teenagers, energy drinks have become an almost ordinary drink, to be consumed before a match, during a study session or simply to imitate adults. In England, however, they will soon no longer be able to be purchased freely by anyone under 16. The British government has confirmed that from April 2027 the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to minors will be banned. The measure has yet to complete parliamentary passage, but the political decision has been made and the executive intends to introduce it through secondary legislation under the Food Safety Act. This is not a ban on any energy drink or, more generally, on all caffeinated drinks. The established threshold is 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter : above this level, the product cannot be sold to under 16s. Tea, coffee and soft drinks with lower concentrations will be excluded. The ban will also affect vending machines and online sales The restriction will be extended to all main commercial channels: supermarkets, small shops, bars, restaurants, cafes, websites and vending machines. Traders will have to verify the age of buyers, while checks will be entrusted to local authorities. Fines could reach up to £2,500. It is an important step because several British chains had already spontaneously adopted limits on sales, but the system left large areas uncovered. A boy could have the can rejected at the supermarket and buy it a few meters later in an independent shop, online or from a vending machine. According to government estimates, approx 100 thousand English children and teenagers consume energy drinks with a high concentration of caffeine every day . Consumption would also be more widespread in families and economically disadvantaged areas, transforming the issue into a problem of health and education inequality. The choice comes after a public consultation held between September and November 2025. 1,095 responses were collected and 90 percent of participants declared themselves in favor of introducing an age limit. Support came mainly from parents, teachers, doctors, local administrations and organizations involved in the protection of minors. More critical, however, is a part of the beverage industry, which considers the measure disproportionate compared to the available scientific evidence. How much caffeine does a can contain A standard 250 milliliter can generally contains approx 80 milligrams of caffeine a quantity similar to that of an espresso. The concentration, however, is around 320 milligrams per liter, more than double the threshold identified by the English government to trigger the ban. Larger formats or particularly concentrated products can provide significantly higher quantities in one go. The problem is not only the absolute value, but the relationship with body weight. The European Food Safety Authority, EFSA, indicates a caffeine level for children and adolescents that does not cause concern at approximately 3 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day considering all food sources. For a 40-kilo boy that means about 120 milligrams daily. A single standard can already provides 80; to this can be added cola, tea, coffee, chocolate and other products containing caffeine. Furthermore, the EFSA reference does not represent a threshold beyond which intoxication automatically occurs, but a prudential level referring to the healthy population. It is precisely this difference that makes the often used comparison between a can and a cup of coffee misleading. Caffeine may be similar, but the audience, consumption patterns and context change: energy drinks are often drunk quickly, in large formats, sometimes in multiple consecutive units and in combination with other sources of stimulants. The effects of energy drinks on sleep, anxiety and the heart Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system and temporarily reduces the perception of tiredness. In more sensitive subjects or when quantities increase it can cause agitation, tremors, headaches, nausea, palpitations, increased blood pressure and difficulty falling asleep. In adolescents, energy drink consumption has been associated with poorer quality sleep, anxiety, gastrointestinal disorders, difficulty concentrating and some acute cardiovascular effects, such as increased heart rate and blood pressure. However, a distinction is necessary on this point. The English government itself recognizes that much of the available research is observational: that is, it shows a relationship between consumption and health problems or academic performance, but does not always allow it to be demonstrated that it was exclusively the drink that caused them. Those who sleep little, lead an irregular lifestyle or exhibit other risky behaviors could, for example, also be more inclined to consume energy drinks. The evidence, therefore, is not definitive. However, they are coherent enough to have pushed London to apply a precautionary principle, especially considering that the product already contains the indication on the label not to recommend it to children. The sugar problem Next to caffeine there is sugar. According to the briefing from the European Parliamentary Research Service, a typical 250 milliliter can can contain approximately 27 grams equivalent to five or six teaspoons. In a single product it is therefore possible to reach or exceed the daily quantity of free sugars indicated as a prudential objective by the World Health Organization. Sugar-free versions eliminate this specific problem, but not the caffeine one. For this reason the English measure is based on the concentration of the stimulant and not on the calories of the drink. Another particularly risky habit is pairing it with alcohol. Caffeine may make a person feel more alert, but it does not reduce blood alcohol levels or restore normal coordination, judgment, or reaction times. The Italian guidelines for healthy eating remind us that the exciting effect of energy drinks can mask, but not cancel, the neurological effects of alcohol. In Europe, six countries have already introduced limits England is not the first European territory to intervene. Lithuania and Latvia introduced bans on sales to minors in 2014 and 2016 respectively. Poland and Romania followed in 2024, while Hungary and Bulgaria adopted restrictions in 2025. The Spanish region of Galicia also banned sales and consumption by minors, partly equating these drinks with alcohol. However, the rules are not uniform: the minimum age, the definition of energy drink, the concentrations considered and the places where sale is prohibited change. At community level there is currently no specific law that prevents teenagers from purchasing them. The European Food Information Regulation requires drinks with more than 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter to clearly display the warning “high caffeine content” and the indication that the product is not recommended for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Brussels still considers the scientific advice published by EFSA in 2015 to be sufficient and has not announced a joint ban. However, Member States remain free to introduce more stringent national rules, provided they are justified. Energy drinks banned in Italy? Not for now In Italy Today there is no national age limit for purchasing energy drinks . A teenager can buy them at the supermarket, at the bar, online or through a vending machine, while the only mandatory protection is represented by the information on the packaging. The English decision will not automatically produce consequences in our country. However, it could reopen the debate on the effectiveness of a simple warning printed in characters that are often not very obvious, especially when the product is promoted through extreme sports, gaming, music, creators and campaigns capable of speaking directly to young people. A possible Italian intervention could follow the English model, limiting only drinks with over 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter, or focus on schools, vending machines, advertising and sponsorships aimed at minors. However, a ban alone would not solve every problem. A study cited by the European Parliament found that in Poland, after the restrictions were introduced, only a minority of children attempting to purchase were subjected to regular age checks. The issue is therefore not to establish that a single can is necessarily dangerous for every teenager. The point is to decide whether a product already declared not recommended for children should continue to be available without any limit, even in large formats and at any time. England chose to answer no. From 2027 the can will remain on the shelves, but to buy it you will need to be at least 16 years old. Now the debate is destined to move to other European countries too, including Italy. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw14.text: Image source, Vatican via Reuters Image caption, Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery By Henry Moore Published 5 hours ago Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications. The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital. Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said. Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next Published 2 days ago On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure. His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung". The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital. Image source, Vatican via Reuters Image caption, The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure. Photograph: Westend61/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September, while the median property price across houses and units remained flat over the year. Photograph: Westend61/Getty Images Housing Mortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them? As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbs Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Fri 16 Oct 2026 19.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 21.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google High rents and falling property prices have opened a rare window for Australian tenants to become homeowners, with mortgage repayments cheaper than rent in dozens of suburbs. Guardian Australia’s analysis of Cotality data shows that median rents in inner-city Melbourne , suburban Canberra and Darwin are now nearly matching weekly home loan repayments. ‘Are they going to fall enough?’ The renters waiting for the house price downturn to change their fortunes Read more In one in 10 suburbs and towns across the country, repayments are less than $200 a week higher than rent, for the typical property. In some suburbs, they are actually cheaper. Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September to reach $713 per week, Cotality data shows. The median property price across houses and units was flat over the year, after six months of steady falls. Is it cheaper to buy or rent in your suburb? Is it cheaper to buy or rent in your suburb? The typical rent for a Melbourne apartment was $628 a week after rising 4.8% over the last year. The typical repayments for a Melbourne flat were $211 more, or $839 a week, based on a median value of $624,740 in September, down nearly $25,000 from a year earlier. The analysis assumes a new 30-year loan of 95% of the value, at a 6.2% interest rate. It does not account for any additional costs. Smaller loans made with bigger deposits would make repayments even more affordable compared with rents. Owner-occupiers purchasing with a 5% deposit would typically do so through the government’s low deposit scheme, which is designed to help first home buyers. Repayments were cheaper than rent for the typical property in Carlton, Melbourne CBD, Notting Hill, Travancore and Southbank. Repayments on new loans had risen overall in the last year for most suburbs, as lower values were offset by interest rates rising 1 percentage point. Where values had fallen more than 10%, though, repayments were likely lower. Clint Waters, a Melbourne mortgage broker, said home buying interest had dropped but renters were inquiring in strong numbers as they weighed lower house prices against higher rents. “They’re certainly doing the maths … [and] the equation at the moment is starting to narrow,” Waters said. Australia’s housing market is definitely in a downturn – but let’s put that in perspective | Hal Pawson Read more Waters, director at Axton Finance, said a stable or growing number were looking to buy direct from their landlord, making the switch without moving. “Landlords are getting slammed left, right and centre, and going ‘screw this, I’m going to offload,’” Waters said. “Tenants will ring us up and say, ‘I need to work out if I’ve got the capacity to buy this thing.’” New apartments pushing down prices In Sydney , repayments were just $100 a week more than rents in inner-city Ultimo and western suburbs Warwick Farm, Rosehill, Liverpool and Granville. In the Canberra suburbs of Belconnen and Phillip, repayments were less than $75 a week more than rents. If only apartments are included, Braddon, Lyons, Gungahlin and Harrison join the list. Gerard Burg, a Cotality researcher, said areas with significant apartment development tended to be cheaper to buy than rent, especially where flats were being sold direct to owner-occupiers and not rented out. “That just [shows] this influx of supply pushing down the value of the purchase, while comparatively tight rental availability had led to this increase in rents,” Burg said. But such areas were “anomalies”, he said. Houses remain generally more expensive to buy than rent. “If it was a sustained thing that you could buy a property more cheaply than renting it, then everyone would buy and everyone would exit the rental market,” Burg said. It was cheaper to buy in a quarter of suburbs in Darwin , where rents have risen 11.6% in the year. Most areas where buying was cheaper than renting were mining or resource project areas in which fly-in fly-out workers temporarily rent rather than buy, Burg said. Burg said mortgage repayments would likely fall if the Reserve Bank held rates steady and values kept falling, as expected by financial markets, potentially narrowing the gap with rents. “[With] rents continuing to increase or … go sideways, that could occur.” Explore more on these topics Housing Business Renting Victoria Melbourne Interest rates Sydney news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Are they going to fall enough?’ The renters waiting for the house price downturn to change their fortunes Rent-tech platforms sidestepping credit card surcharge ban with new fees and paid ‘memberships’ Unemployment in Australia reaches 4.7%, its highest in nearly five years Tax changes to discretionary trusts are likely on the way – what is happening and why are people upset?
